==English==
{{wp}}

===Etymology===
{{ety|en|:inh|enm:trade<ety:der<gml: trade<ety:der<osx:trada>>>>|tree=+}}
From {{inh|en|enm|trade|t=path, course of conduct}}, introduced into English by Hanseatic merchants, from {{der|en|gml|trade|t=track, course}}, from {{der|en|osx|trada|t=spoor, track}}, from {{der|en|gmw-pro|*tradu}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*tradō|t=track, way}}, and cognate with {{cog|ang|tredan|t=to tread}}; ultimately from {{der|en|ine-pro|*dreh₂-|t=to tread, walk, step, run}}. {{displaced|enm|chaffare}}.

Cognate with {{cog|nl|trade}}, {{m|nl|tra|t=path, trail, course, trade}}, {{cog|nds-de|Traad|t=track, wagon trail}}, {{cog|lb|Tratt|t=step, pace}}, {{cog|is|tröð|t=a lane between fences, enclosure, pen}}.

===Pronunciation===

* {{audio|en|En-uk-trade.ogg|a=RP}}
* {{audio|en|LL-Q1860 (eng)-Naomi Persephone Amethyst (NaomiAmethyst)-trade.wav|a=GA}}

* {{rhymes|en|eɪd|s=1}}

===Noun===
{{en-noun|~}}

# {{lb|en|uncountable}} The [[buying]] and [[selling]] of [[goods]] and [[services]] on a [[market]].
#: {{syn|en|commerce}}
# {{lb|en|countable}} A particular instance of [[buy]]ing or [[sell]]ing, or a series of related transactions executed as a single investment.
#: {{syn|en|deal|barter}}
#: {{ux|en|I did no '''trades''' with them once the rumors started.}}
# {{lb|en|countable}} An idea or strategy for an investment on a market.
#: {{ux|en|"Sell America" is the latest '''trade''' on Wall Street.}}
# {{lb|en|countable}} An instance of [[barter]]ing items in [[exchange]] for one another.
# {{lb|en|countable}} Those who [[perform]] a particular kind of [[skilled]] work.
#: {{syn|en|business}}
#: {{ux|en|The skilled '''trades''' were the first to organize modern labor unions.}}
# {{lb|en|countable}} Those engaged in an industry or group of related industries.
#: {{ux|en|It is not a retail showroom. It is only for the '''trade'''.}}
# {{senseid|en|skilled practice of a practical occupation}} {{lb|en|countable}} The skilled practice of a practical [[occupation]].
#: {{syn|en|craft}}
#: {{ux|en|He learned his '''trade''' as an [[apprentice]].}}
# {{lb|en|countable|or|uncountable}} An [[occupation]] in the [[secondary sector]], as opposed to an [[agricultural]], [[professional]] or [[military]] one.
#: {{ux|en|After failing his entrance exams, he decided to go into a '''trade'''.}}
#: {{ux|en|Most veterans went into '''trade''' when the war ended.}}
# {{lb|en|uncountable|UK}} The [[business]] given to a [[commercial]] [[establishment]] by its customers.
#: {{syn|en|business|takings|custom|footfall|patronage}}
#: {{ux|en|Even before noon there was considerable '''trade'''.}}
#: {{ux|en|'''Trade''' has been down in this cold weather.}}
#: {{ux|en|The gift shop relies on passing '''trade''' from tourists.}}
# {{lb|en|mostly|in the plural}} [[steady|Steady]] [[wind]]s blowing from east to west above and below the [[equator]].
#: {{ux|en|They rode the '''trades''' going west.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1826|author=James Horsburgh|title=India Directory, Or Directions for Sailing to and from the East Indies, China, New Holland, Cape of Good Hope, Brazil and the Interjacent Ports|page=28|text=Calms and variable winds, are also experienced during every month of the year, in the space between the '''trades''';{{...}} the vicinity of the north-east '''trade''' seems most liable to them.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ctJYAAAAcAAJ&pg=PA28|origyear=1816}}
# {{lb|en|only as plural}} A publication intended for participants in an industry or related group of industries.
#: {{ux|en|Rumors about layoffs are all over the '''trades'''.}}
# {{lb|en|uncountable|gay slang}} A [[masculine]] man available for [[casual sex]] with men, often for pay. {{non-gloss|(Compare ''[[rough trade]]''.)}}
#: {{ux|en|Not you tryna impress plumber '''trade'''.}}
#: {{ux|en|Josh picked up some '''trade''' last night.}}
# {{lb|en|obsolete|uncountable}} Instruments of any occupation.
# {{short for|en|trade paperback}}
# {{lb|en|mining}} Refuse or rubbish from a mine.
# {{lb|en|obsolete}} A track or trail; a way; a path; [[passage]].
# {{lb|en|obsolete}} A course; a custom; a practice; an occupation.
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1655|author=w:Philip Massinger; {{w|John Fletcher (playwright)|John Fletcher}}|title=w:A Very Woman|passage=Long did I love this lady, / Long was my travel, long my '''trade''' to win her.}}
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare Measure|III|i|passage=Thy sin's not accidental but a '''trade'''.}}

===Verb===
{{en-verb}}

# {{lb|en|ambitransitive}} To [[engage]] in [[#Noun|trade]]. {{+obj|en|&transitive/:in<something> + :with<somebody>}}
#: {{syn|en|deal}}
#: {{ux|en|This company '''trades''' (in) precious metal.}}
#: {{ux|en|He withdrew money to his bank account after several years of '''trading''' stocks on E-Trade.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1727|author=John Arbuthnot|title=Tables of Ancient Coins, Weights and Measures|page=248|text={{...}}a free port, where Nations warring with one another resorted with their Goods, and '''traded''' as in a neutral Country.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UmBMAAAAcAAJ&pg=PA248}}
# {{lb|en|finance|intransitive|copulative}} To be traded at a certain price or under certain conditions.
#: {{ux|en|Apple is '''trading''' at $200.}}
#: {{ux|en|ExxonMobil '''trades''' on the NYSE.}}
#: {{ux|en|The stock is '''trading''' rich relative to its sector.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive|with '''for'''}} To give (something) in [[exchange]] (for).
#: {{syn|en|exchange|swap|switch|truck|id4=trade}}
#: {{ux|en|Will you '''trade''' your precious watch for my earring?}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[mutually]] [[exchange]] (something) (with).
#: {{ux|en|The rival schoolboys '''traded''' insults and punches.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive|with '''on'''}} To use or exploit a particular aspect, such as a name, reputation, or image, to gain advantage or benefit.
#: {{syn|en|exploit|[[capitalize]] on|[[take advantage]] of|use|leverage|[[benefit]] from|[[make use]] of|milk}}
#: {{ux|en|Some musicians try to '''trade on''' their past success by playing the same hits over and over again.}}
# {{lb|en|gardening|transitive|or|intransitive}} To [[give]] someone a [[plant]] and [[receive]] a [[different]] one in [[return]].
# {{lb|en|ambitransitive}} To do business; offer for sale as for one's [[livelihood]].
#: {{syn|en|do business}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To have dealings; to be concerned or associated (with).
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare Macbeth|III|v|passage=Saucy and over bold, how did you dare / To '''trade''' and traffic with Macbeth}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[recommend]] and get [[recommendation]]s.
#: {{syn|en|exchange}}

====Verb====
{{en-verb|~s|~ing|brought,brang<l:colloquial,dialectal>|brought,brung<l:colloquial,dialectal>,broughten<l:rare,dialectal>}}

# {{lb|en|transitive|ditransitive}} To [[transport]] toward somebody/somewhere.
#: {{ux|en|Waiter, please '''bring''' me a single malt whiskey.}}
#* {{RQ:Besant Ivory Gate|II
|passage=At twilight in the summer{{...}}the mice come out. They{{...}}eat the luncheon crumbs. Mr. Checkly, for instance, always '''brought''' his dinner in a paper parcel in his coat-tail pocket, and ate it when so disposed, sprinkling crumbs lavishly{{...}}on the floor.}}
#* {{RQ:Allingham China Governess|chapter=5|passage=A waiter '''brought''' his aperitif, which was a small scotch and soda, and as he sipped it gratefully he sighed. ¶ ‘Civilized,’ he said to Mr. Campion. ‘Humanizing.’{{...}}‘Cigars and summer days and women in big hats with swansdown face-powder, that's what it reminds me of.’}}
#* {{RQ:Guardian|date=21 August 2012| author=Ed Pilkington| title=Death penalty on trial: should Reggie Clemons live or die?| url=http://www.guardian.co.uk/world/2012/aug/21/death-penalty-trial-reggie-clemons?| passage=Next month, Clemons will be '''brought''' before a court presided over by a "special master", who will review the case one last time.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive|figuratively}} To [[supply]] or [[contribute]].
#: {{ux|en|The new company director '''brought''' a fresh perspective on sales and marketing.}}
#* {{RQ:Hough Purchase Price|chapter=I|text=“{{...}}it is not fair of you to '''bring''' against mankind double weapons ! Dangerous enough you are as woman alone, without '''bringing''' to your aid those gifts of mind suited to problems which men have been accustomed to arrogate to themselves.”}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[occasion]] or [[bring about]].
#: {{ux|en|Let's '''bring''' our differences to an issue.}}
#: {{ux|en|The controversial TV broadcast '''brought''' a storm of complaints.}}
#: {{ux|en|Seeing her '''brought''' the memories flooding back and tears to my eyes.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[raise]] (a lawsuit, charges, etc.) against somebody.
#* {{RQ:Economist|date=2013-08-10| volume=408| issue=8848| title=[http://www.economist.com/news/leaders/21583277-worlds-biggest-polluter-going-green-it-needs-speed-up-transition-can-china Can China clean up fast enough?]| passage=It has jailed environmental activists and is planning to limit the power of judicial oversight by handing a state-approved body a monopoly over '''bringing''' environmental lawsuits.}}
# To persuade; to induce; to draw; to lead; to guide.
#* {{RQ:Locke Human Understanding|2|11|text=It seems so preposterous a thing{{...}}that they do not easily '''bring''' themselves to it.}}
# To produce in exchange; to sell for; to fetch.
#: {{ux|en|What does coal '''bring''' per ton?}}
# {{lb|en|baseball}} To pitch, often referring to a particularly hard thrown [[fastball]].
#: {{ux|en|The [[closer]] Jones can really '''bring''' it.}}
# {{lb|en|chess}} To move a [[piece]] into a more active position, esp. to initially [[develop]] it.
#: {{ux|en|You want to '''bring''' the rook and then start pushing your pawns.}}

===Etymology 1===
{{etymon|en|:inh|enm:flowe<ety:from<enm:flowen>>|id=noun|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|flowe}}, from the verb (see below). The psychology sense “state of focus” was {{coin|en|Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi|in=1975|nocap=1|nocat=1}}.
[[File:Jõelähtme_jõgi._01.jpg|thumb|]]

====Noun====
{{en-noun|~}}

# Movement in people or things characterized with a continuous motion, involving either a non solid mass or a multitude.
# The movement of a [[real]] or [[figurative]] [[fluid]].
#* {{RQ:Churchill Celebrity|IV|48|Mr. Cooke at once began a tirade against the residents of Asquith for permitting a sandy and generally disgraceful condition of the roads. So roundly did he vituperate the inn management in particular, and with such a loud '''flow''' of words, that I trembled lest he should be heard on the veranda.}}
# {{lb|en|math}} A [[formalization]] of the idea of the [[motion]] of [[particle]]s in a [[fluid]], as a [[group]] [[action]] of the [[real number]]s on a [[set]].
#: {{uxa|en|The notion of '''flow''' is basic to the study of ordinary differential equations.}}
# The rising movement of the [[tide]].
# [[smoothness|Smoothness]] or [[continuity]].
#: {{uxa|en|The room was small, but it had good symmetry and '''flow'''.}}
# The amount of a fluid that moves or the rate of fluid movement.
#: {{uxa|en|Turn on the valve and make sure you have sufficient '''flow'''.}}
#: {{uxa|en|Other devices measure water '''flow''' in streams fed by melted ice.}}
# A flow pipe, carrying liquid away from a boiler or other central plant (compare with [[return]] pipe which returns fluid to central plant).
# {{sid|en|mental state}} {{lb|en|psychology}} A mental state characterized by [[concentration]], [[focus]]{{,}} and enjoyment of a given task.
#* {{RQ:Guardian|url=http://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/the-running-blog/2014/jan/14/achieve-state-flow-running-perform-best|title=How to achieve a state of flow when running|date=2014-01-14|author=Alex Lockwood|passage=The point about '''flow''' is that it is enjoyable. # The [[emission]] of [[blood]] during [[menstruation]].
#: {{uxa|en|Tampons can be small or large, slender or thick. From “slender” to “super”, you can pick the size that matches your '''flow'''.}}

===Etymology 3===
{{ety|en|id=bog}}
{{unc|en}}. Perhaps from {{cog|non|flói|t=a large bay, firth}}, see {{m|en|floe}}. Compare {{cog|sco|flow|t=peat-bog, marsh}}, {{cog|is|flói|t=marshy ground}}.

====Noun====
{{en-noun}}

# {{lb|en|Scotland}} A [[bog]] or [[mire]], especially a rough, waterlogged one.
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1794|author=John Sinclair|title=The Statistical Account of Scotland|volume=10|page=328
|passage={{...}} there are other extensive mosses in this district, commonly called flowes, which it is not probable ever will, or ever can be, converted into arable land. Some of these '''flowes''' are found to be 20, 25, or 30 feet deep, and are, besides, such a dead level, that the water has little or no descent; and even supposing they should be cast, or burnt to the bottom, standing pools of dirty water could only stand in their place.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1871|author=Alexander Boswell|title=Poetical Works|page=213
|passage=Ye'll stick in some '''flow''', Or, ye'll melt in a thow}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1896|author=Proudlock|title=Borderland Muse|page=8
|passage=Dandering o'er ferney knowes, [...] Springing o'er bogs an' '''flowes''', [...]}}

====Usage notes====
* In older forms of English, when the pronoun ''[[thou]]'' was in active use, and verbs used ''[[-est]]'' for distinct second-person singular indicative forms, the verb ''call'' had the form ''[[callest]]'', and had ''[[calledst]]'' for its past tense.
* Similarly, when the ending ''[[-eth]]'' was in active use for third-person singular present indicative forms, the form ''[[calleth]]'' was used.
* The sense of naming an object, as with the phrase ''it’s called a(n)'', is intended to humiliate a listener when the object is known to be familiar:
*: {{usex|en|Hey, here’s something to keep you dry in the rain. It’s '''called''' an umbrella.}}

In the real world, “'''developer'''” and “programmer” can seem almost interchangeable. But in the world of government statistics, where we have legal permanent residency, there’s a clear distinction. In the [US] government’s schema, programmers do the grunt work while the much more numerous — and much faster-growing — software '''developers''' enjoy a broader remit. They figure out what clients need, design solutions and work with folks such as programmers and hardware engineers to implement them. Their pay reflects this gap in responsibilities. The median programmer earned $99,700 in 2023, compared with $132,270 for the median '''developer'''. And while 27.5 percent of programming jobs vanished, jobs for '''developers''' have only fallen 0.3 percent, similar to the broader industry.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20250723162050/https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2025/03/14/programming-jobs-lost-artificial-intelligence/|archivedate=23 July 2025}}

From {{inh|en|enm|receyven}}, from {{der|en|fro|recevoir|receivre}}, from {{der|en|la|recipiō|recipere|t=take back, accept, etc.}}, from {{m|la|re-||back}} + {{m|la|capiō||to take}}; see [[capacious]].
